A · The FFT Key Terms — Doing It Fast

FFT

/ˌef.efˈtiː/ · Fast Fourier Transform

An algorithm that computes the DFT. Not a different transform — a faster route to the same numbers.

อัลกอริทึมที่คำนวณ DFT ให้เร็วขึ้น — ไม่ใช่การแปลงคนละแบบ ผลลัพธ์เหมือนกันเป๊ะ

Time complexity

/kəmˈpleks.ɪ.ti/ · written O(⋅)

How the work grows with the input size — the thing you already study in algorithms.

งานเพิ่มขึ้นอย่างไรเมื่อข้อมูลใหญ่ขึ้น (เรื่องเดียวกับวิชาอัลกอริทึม)

Divide and conquer

/dɪˈvaɪd ənd ˈkɒŋ.kə/

Split the problem in half, solve both halves, combine cheaply. Merge sort's trick, applied here.

แบ่งครึ่ง แก้ทีละครึ่ง แล้วรวมกลับด้วยงานน้อย — กลวิธีเดียวกับ merge sort

Radix-2

/ˈreɪ.dɪks tuː/

The common FFT that halves repeatedly, so it likes N to be a power of two.

FFT แบบแบ่งครึ่งซ้ำ ๆ จึงชอบให้ N เป็นกำลังของสอง

📌

Say this one out loud, because it is the most common misconception in the whole course: the FFT is not an approximation and not a different tool. It is the DFT of Session 6, computed cleverly.

A · The FFT The definition does the same work over and over
X[k]=n=0∑N−1​x[n]⋅wkn

small x = a sample in time · capital X = a bin in frequency

N samples in, N bins out — which is why the table is square.

Row k × column n holds wkn — the probe x[n] gets for bin k.

Last cell: kn=3×3=9, and 9 mod 4 = 1 → −j again.

One bin, worked out — row k=1 against x=[1,0,−1,0]:

X[1] = 1(1) + 0(−j) + (−1)(−1) + 0(j) = 2

those four probes are row k=1 of the table

💡

Wherever an algorithm recomputes the same thing, a faster one is waiting — cashing that in is the next two slides.

1 / 60
A · The FFT Split the samples into evens and odds

① Split by position

the split at N=4, x=[1,2,3,4] — nothing zero in it

evens x[0],x[2] = 1, 3
odds  x[1],x[3] = 2, 4

no arithmetic yet

same tree as above, run at N=4 — that is the 2 levels in the bar below

→

② One DFT per half

a 2-point DFT is only a
sum and a difference:
E[0] = 1+3 = 4   E[1] = 1−3 = −2
O[0] = 2+4 = 6   O[1] = 2−4 = −2

each half is only N/2=2 long, so k runs 0, 1 — there is no k = 2 or 3 down here

Four numbers, but not the answer yet — E and O describe half the samples each. Step ③ is what turns them into bins.

→

③ Stitch — one pass of N multiply-adds

top half X[k]=E[k]+wkO[k]
bottom    X[k+N/2]=E[k]−wkO[k]

k=0…N/2−1 → here k = 0, 1 · k+N/2=k+2 · from slide 6's circle: w0=1, w1=−j

k=0 X[0] = E[0] + w⁰O[0] = 4 + (1)(6) = 10
k=1 X[1] = E[1] + w¹O[1] = −2 + (−j)(−2) = −2+2j
k=0 X[2] = E[0] − w⁰O[0] = 4 − (1)(6) = −2
k=1 X[3] = E[1] − w¹O[1] = −2 − (−j)(−2) = −2−2j

X = [10, −2+2j, −2, −2−2j] — exactly np.fft.fft([1,2,3,4])

direct: each of 4 bins × all 4 samples = N2 = 16
this way: 2 levels × one sweep of 4 = Nlog2​N = 8

⚠️

Caching the probes is not the trick — naive_dft caches them all, still thousands of times slower. E and O are what get reused.

1 / 60
A · The FFT Halving log2​N times, N work each time
N2⟶Nlog2​N

The rule from slide 7: one stitch that produces a result of length L costs L multiply-adds — and L is simply the number in “DFT of L”.

Slide 7's tree, counted — smallest pieces first:

levelyou buildhow manycost each = Lthis level
1DFT of 2428
2DFT of 4248
3DFT of 8188
total for 3 levels → 24

Those counts are the boxes on slide 7 — four DFT of 2, two DFT of 4, one DFT of 8. Half as many each level, each one twice as big: (N/L)×L=N every time.

N = 8    8 × 3 (levels)     = 24     · 8² = 64
N = 1024 1024 × 10 (levels) = 10,240 · 1024² = 1,048,576
🧠

If merge sort's NlogN feels familiar, it should — the same recursion, spent on a different problem.

1 / 60
A · The FFT What if N will not halve?

Slide 7 halved 8 into 4 into 2 — but recordings do not arrive in powers of two. Three seconds at 44,100 Hz is 132,300 samples. So stop asking whether N is a power of two, and ask what it factors into:

4096 = 212

halves 12 times ✓

Textbook radix-2 — slide 7's tree, twelve levels deep.

4000 = 25 · 53

splits into 2s, then 5s ✓

Halving runs out after five levels, so it splits into fives instead. Same recursion.

4093 = prime

nothing divides it ✗

The recursion has nowhere to go. This is the awkward size — not 4000.

🔑

Small factors are what matter — not a power of two. np.fft.fft factors N itself and splits by whatever it finds (mixed-radix). Only a prime leaves nothing to find, and even that fallback is still NlogN — a worse constant, not a return to N2.

If your N is awkward, three ways out — and each one charges you something:

the fix what you write what it costs
Pad up with zeros np.fft.fft(x, n=4096) The bins move: spacing becomes fs​/4096, not fs​/4093. Zeros carry no information, so the spectrum is interpolated, not sharpened.
Trim down np.fft.fft(x[:4000]) Nothing invented — but you throw real samples away, and a shorter signal buys a coarser Δf.
Pick N when you capture frame = 256 · 512 · 1024 Nothing at all — the problem never arises. This is why every spectrogram window in sub-topic B is a power of two.

⏱️ All three are timed for real on slide 14 — where the interesting question turns out not to be the speed.

A · The FFT 🌍 What became possible when this got fast

🎧

Audio you use daily

Find what you cannot hear, then throw it away.

2,450

FFTs a second

one audio channel

🏥

Medical imaging

An MRI measures frequencies. The image is one FFT away.

512

FFTs per image

256 rows + 256 columns

📡

Every wireless link

Hundreds of frequencies at once — one FFT per symbol.

250,000

FFTs a second

one Wi-Fi stream

Same routine every time — only the count changes. At N2 none of these would run at all.

🏆

Cooley and Tukey, 1965 — Gauss had it in 1805 and nobody noticed. The most important numerical algorithm of our lifetime, and the numbers above are why.

1 / 60
A · The FFT ↩ So where did the time go?

Both bars are the same DFT — only the route differs.

Slide 4 measured about 10⁴×. The operation count explains 341× of it — the rest is the probe table the definition has to build and stream, which the FFT never materialises at all.

nothing was approximated · nothing was skipped

The time went into repetition. Only N different probe values exist, yet the definition rebuilds the same partial sums from scratch for every one of the N bins.

The FFT arranges the work so each partial sum is computed once and reused — log2​N levels deep.

🔁

Which means the answer to "should I use the DFT or the FFT?" is: you already are using the FFT. np.fft has never done anything else.

1 / 60
A · The FFT
💻 LAB — Race the definition against the library
①Write the DFT as its definition · ② check both agree · ③ time them
lab_a.pyColab · no downloads needed
import numpy as np, time
def naive_dft(x):
    N = len(x); n = np.arange(N)
    return np.exp(-2j*np.pi*np.outer(n, n)/N) @ x     # the definition, verbatim

x = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=1024)
print("same answer?", np.allclose(naive_dft(x), np.fft.fft(x)))
t0 = time.perf_counter(); naive_dft(x); slow = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(300): np.fft.fft(x)
fast = (time.perf_counter() - t0)/300
print(f"naive {slow*1e3:.1f} ms · fft {fast*1e3:.4f} ms · {slow/fast:.0f}x")
✅

same answer? True, then roughly 17 ms vs 0.010 ms — about 1800×. Your numbers will differ; the ratio will not be small. Even this "naive" version is a fast matrix multiply — a Python loop would be slower still.

1 / 60
A · The FFT 🔍 Explore — double N and watch the two curves separate
explore_a.py
for N in [256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096]:
    x = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=N)
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); naive_dft(x); slow = time.perf_counter() - t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(300): np.fft.fft(x)
    fast = (time.perf_counter() - t0)/300
    print(N, "|", round(slow*1e3, 1), "ms |", round(fast*1e3, 4), "ms |",
          round(slow/fast), "x")
🔎

Measured here: 218× · 743× · 1779× · 5260× · 11938×. Read the pattern rather than the numbers — each doubling of N roughly quadruples the naive time and only slightly more than doubles the FFT's, so the gap itself keeps growing. That is what a difference in complexity class looks like when you can see it.

A · The FFT 🎯 Your Turn — the awkward sizes
🎯

Predict first: a prime leaves nothing to split. How much slower — and where does 4000 land?

your_turn_a.pyruns as-is · predict before you run it
import numpy as np, time
def ms(N, pad=None):
    x = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=N); np.fft.fft(x, n=pad)   # warm-up
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(200): np.fft.fft(x, n=pad)
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 200 * 1e3
for N in (4096, 4093, 4000): print(N, round(ms(N), 4), "ms")   # 2¹², prime, 2⁵·5³
print("4093 padded to 4096", round(ms(4093, 4096), 4), "ms")
✅

What you should see: the prime is about 6× slower — nothing halves, so the library falls back on a general algorithm. 4000 lands with 4096, not with the prime — it factors as 2⁵·5³, which is slide 9's rule holding up under measurement. Padding is fast again but not free: the bins now sit at fs​/4096, not fs​/4093. Your sentence: what did padding change about the result, not the speed?

B · The Spectrogram Key Terms — Short-Time Analysis

STFT

/ˌes.tiː.efˈtiː/ · Short-Time Fourier Transform

Cut the signal into short frames and transform each one. That is the entire idea.

ตัดสัญญาณเป็นช่วงสั้น ๆ แล้ว FFT ทีละช่วง — แค่นั้นจริง ๆ

Xi​[k]=FFT(x[i⋅hop…i⋅hop+L−1])

Frame / window length (L)

/freɪm/

How many samples go into one FFT. Everything inside a frame is treated as if it happened at once.

จำนวน sample ต่อหนึ่งเฟรม · ของทุกอย่างในเฟรมถือว่าเกิดพร้อมกัน

Δf=fs​/L · Δt=L/fs​ — sub-topic D

Hop / overlap

/hɒp/

How far the frame slides each step. Frames usually overlap so nothing falls between them.

ระยะเลื่อนของเฟรม · ปกติให้ซ้อนกันเพื่อไม่ให้เหตุการณ์ตกร่อง

hop=L−overlap · one column every hop/fs​ s

Spectrogram

/spekˈtrɒɡ.rəm/

The stack of those spectra drawn as an image: time across, frequency up, strength as colour.

ภาพที่เอาสเปกตรัมของทุกเฟรมมาเรียงกัน — แกนนอนเวลา แกนตั้งความถี่ สีคือความแรง

S[k,i]=∣Xi​[k]∣ · fk​=kfs​/L · ti​=ihop/fs​

🔑

Nothing new is computed — the FFT fills in the colour S only; both axes are arithmetic on fs​, L and hop.

1 / 60
B · The Spectrogram Cut into frames · transform each · stack the columns
🧱

Cutting the signal into frames and transforming each one is the STFT — the term from the previous slide, and the whole of it. Three steps, and you already know the middle one: ① take L samples ② run the FFT ③ paint the magnitudes as one vertical stripe. Slide along and repeat. Real frames slide by less than L, so they overlap — slide 19 shows what that buys.

1 / 60
B · The Spectrogram A column is a Session-6 spectrum, turned on its side
1

A spectrum already uses both of its axes: frequency across, strength up.

2

To fit time in, we give up the height axis and encode strength as colour instead.

3

That frees the horizontal axis, and frequency stands up along the vertical.

🎨

Read the decibel range before you read the picture. Most of the spectrograms here span 70 dB below the brightest colour, so a colour halfway up is not half as strong — it is about 2% as strong. Always print a colour bar on your own plots; sub-topic C shows why.

1 / 60
B · The Spectrogram Why the frames overlap
🔗

With no overlap, an event that straddles a frame boundary is split between two columns and looks weaker than it was: the tap reads 7 dB over the hum on the left and 25 dB on the right. Sliding the frame by a quarter of its length (75% overlap) is the usual default — it costs four times the computation, which is affordable precisely because of sub-topic A.

1 / 60
B · The Spectrogram Put real numbers on both axes

you supply

fs = 8000 Hz  ·  L = 256  ·  hop = 64

— the FFT supplies none of these, and the axes are arithmetic from here on

↕ the vertical axis — Hz

row spacing  Δf=fs​/L=8000/256= 31.25 Hz

rows run k=0…L/2=128 → 129 rows, reaching fs​/2= 4000 Hz

any row:  fk​=k⋅Δf

and backwards — which row is 1000 Hz?

k=fL/fs​=1000×256/8000= row 32  ✓ 32 × 31.25 = 1000

↔ the horizontal axis — seconds

a new column every  hop/fs​=64/8000= 8 ms

any column:  ti​=i⋅8 ms

but each column still sees  Δt=L/fs​= 32 ms of signal

how many columns from a 2-second clip (16,000 samples)?

(16000−256)/64+1= 247 columns

Z.shape = (129, 247)

Lab B prints exactly this on slide 24 — and you just worked it out before running anything.

⚠️

8 ms and 32 ms are not the same thing. One 6 ms tap lands in L/hop=4 frames, so it lights 4 columns — 32 ms wide. More overlap draws more columns; only L moves the blur, and that knob is sub-topic D.

B · The Spectrogram 🌍 Use case: the fault that only exists after 1.6 seconds
⚙️

Session 6 could have found that 1450 Hz tone — but only as "there is some 1450 Hz in this recording", with no idea it arrived partway through. Here you can see the moment it starts, which is the difference between "this machine has a problem" and "this machine's problem starts at 1.6 s". The second one is a timestamp you can take to the operating log — whatever the machine was doing at 1.6 s is now your suspect.

1 / 60
B · The Spectrogram ↩ Why one spectrum could not tell you the tune

One spectrum

answers "which frequencies are in this recording?" — all five notes are in there, it reports all five, and it was never asked when.

rfft(all 2.25 s) → 9,001 bins

one column · no time axis at all

Many short spectra

answer "which frequencies are in this moment?" — same transform, asked more often. Lined up in time, they are the spectrogram.

spectrogram(L=256) → (129, 278)

278 answers instead of one

So why keep ③? Six curves already crowd — 278 will not fit. Colour buys the room, and what returns is an image a model can be fed (sub-topic C).

⏱️

And notice the cost of the trick: each column now describes a slice, not an instant. Anything that happens inside one frame is smeared across it — which is the subject of sub-topic D.

B · The Spectrogram
💻 LAB — Your first spectrogram
①Build a sweep · ② one call · ③ read the diagonal
lab_b.pyColab · no downloads needed
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal
fs = 8000; t = np.arange(0, 2, 1/fs)
x = signal.chirp(t, f0=200, t1=2, f1=3000)      # a rising sweep
f, tt, Z = signal.spectrogram(x, fs, nperseg=256,
                              noverlap=192, mode="magnitude")
plt.pcolormesh(tt, f, 20*np.log10(Z + 1e-8), shading="gouraud")
plt.ylabel("Hz"); plt.xlabel("s"); plt.colorbar(label="dB"); plt.show()
print(Z.shape, "= (frequency bins, time frames)")
✅

A clean diagonal from bottom-left to top-right, and (129, 247) printed — 129 frequency bins by 247 time frames. Those two numbers are worth pausing on: you just turned a 16,000-sample recording into a 129 × 247 image.

1 / 60
B · The Spectrogram 🔍 Explore — what the frame length does to the shape
explore_b.py
for L in [64, 256, 1024]:
    f, tt, Z = signal.spectrogram(x, fs, nperseg=L, noverlap=3*L//4,
                                  mode="magnitude")
    print(f"L={L:5d} | shape {Z.shape} | Δf = {fs/L:6.1f} Hz"
          f" | Δt = {1000*L/fs:6.1f} ms")
🔎

Shapes (33, 997) · (129, 247) · (513, 59) — the middle one is exactly what the Run printed: same L, same 75% hop. Look at what is being traded: a longer frame buys you rows (frequency detail) and spends columns (time detail), and the total number of cells barely changes (32,901 · 31,863 · 30,267). The picture is not getting better or worse — it is getting rotated between two kinds of sharpness. Sub-topic D puts a formula on that.

B · The Spectrogram 🎯 Your Turn — draw a signal you can recognise
🎯

Predict first: how many lines will the spectrogram have, and where do they jump?

your_turn_b.pyruns as-is · predict before you run it
t1 = np.arange(0, 1, 1/fs);  NOTES = (440, 880, 660, 1320)
a = np.sin(2*np.pi*440*t1) + 0.5*np.sin(2*np.pi*880*t1)    # 1 s
b = np.sin(2*np.pi*660*t1) + 0.5*np.sin(2*np.pi*1320*t1)   # 1 s
y = np.concatenate([a, b])
f, tt, Z = signal.spectrogram(y, fs, nperseg=1024, noverlap=768, mode="magnitude")
plt.pcolormesh(tt, f, 20*np.log10(Z+1e-8)); plt.ylim(0, 1600); plt.show()
for lab, lo, hi in (("0-1 s", .1, .9), ("1-2 s", 1.1, 1.9)):
    c = Z[:, (tt >= lo) & (tt < hi)].mean(axis=1) / Z.max()
    print(lab, [f"{hz}:{c[np.argmin(abs(f-hz))]:.2f}" for hz in NOTES])
X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(y))*2/len(y); F = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(y), 1/fs)
print("all  ", [f"{hz}:{X[np.argmin(abs(F-hz))]:.2f}" for hz in NOTES])
✅

What you should see: four lines jumping cleanly at t = 1 s. 0-1 s prints 440:1.00 880:0.48 660:0.00 1320:0.00, 1-2 s the mirror image, all every one of the four non-zero — all four, all correct, every zero gone. Your sentence: what did the single spectrum still get right, and what did it lose?

C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model Key Terms — What You Are Looking At

Harmonic stack

/hɑːˈmɒn.ɪk/

Evenly spaced horizontal lines. The spacing is the pitch; the lines are its multiples.

เส้นแนวนอนเรียงห่างเท่า ๆ กัน · ระยะห่างคือระดับเสียง

Transient

/ˈtræn.zi.ənt/

A short burst — a click, a drum hit, a door. Appears as a vertical stripe across all frequencies.

เสียงสั้น ๆ ฉับพลัน · ปรากฏเป็นแถบแนวตั้งพาดทุกความถี่

Chirp / sweep

/tʃɜːp/

A frequency that slides. Appears as a diagonal — the steeper it is, the faster the slide.

ความถี่ที่ไล่ขึ้นหรือลง · ปรากฏเป็นเส้นทแยง

Feature

/ˈfiː.tʃər/

Whatever array you hand a model instead of raw data. A spectrogram is one — an image-shaped one.

ข้อมูลที่แปลงแล้วป้อนโมเดลแทนข้อมูลดิบ · spectrogram คือ feature รูปแบบภาพ

🔑

Three names for shapes that change, plus the plain horizontal line of something steady — four in all, on the next slide. If you can name what you see, you can decide what to measure — and if it looks like an image, you already know a family of models that eat images.

1 / 60
C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model Four shapes cover most of what you will ever see
👁️

Horizontal = something steady · vertical = something sudden · diagonal = something sliding · stacked = something with a pitch. Almost every real recording is a mixture of those four, and naming them is most of what "reading a spectrogram" means in practice.
A diagonal is not many frequencies at once. Read one column of it and you get a single bright bin — one frequency at that instant — which walks upward as time passes. Its slope is the sweep rate: this one climbs 2 330 Hz per second.

1 / 60
C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model A voice is two parts: a buzz, and the mouth that shapes it

pitch = the spacing

How fast the vocal folds buzz — the wave repeats 120 times a second. It is not the loudest line: in “ah” the strongest is 720 Hz, 15 dB above it. Pitch is the spacing, and the mouth decides the brightness.

formants = the humps

The frequencies the mouth amplifies. 700 · 1220 · 2600 Hz is an “ah”; move them to 300 · 2300 · 3000 and the same buzz becomes an “ee”.

timbre = their pattern

Which humps, and where. This — not the pitch — is the difference between "ah" and "ee".

🗣️

Two organs, two knobs, neither touching the other. Move the buzz → lines slide, humps stay: same word, different voice. Reshape the mouth → lines stay, humps move: same note, different picture — “ah” versus “ee”. Speech recognition reads the humps; speaker recognition reads the spacing.

1 / 60
C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model This is the point where DSP hands over to machine learning

audio classification is usually image classification, one transform later

⚠️

Before the model sees it: values go to decibels, 20log10​∣X[k]∣ (a tenth of the peak is −20 dB), and the frequency axis is often warped to a mel scale. Both are your choices, and both change what the model can learn.

1 / 60
C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model 🌍 Use case: how a phone recognises a song in five seconds
🎵

Song identification does not compare audio, or even spectrograms. It keeps only the peaks — the dots on the right — and hashes pairs of them into a database key. Those dots survive background noise, a bad speaker and a phone microphone, because a peak stays a peak — measured here: all 34 come back when the music is played 26 dB quieter, 19 of 34 under noise as loud as itself (the right-hand panel), 11 even through a speaker that passes only 300–1200 Hz. The whole trick is choosing a feature that throws away everything fragile.

1 / 60
C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model ↩ What changed between the two vowels?

The pitch did not change. Both “ah” and “ee” have a bar at every multiple of 120 Hz — the same seven bars above, because the vocal folds never stopped buzzing at 120.

What moved were the humps. The mouth changed shape, so a different set of harmonics got amplified: the low hump fell 700 → 300 Hz, the next rose 1220 → 2300 Hz. That is why the same seven bars come out at different heights.

🤖

And a machine notices it the same way you just did — by looking at where the bright regions are in the picture. The bottom panel is that picture, the arrows are what you both look at, and it is a 129 × 247 array of numbers. Which is precisely why this problem gets handed to a vision model.

1 / 60
C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model
💻 LAB — Turn audio into a model-ready array
①Transform · ② go to dB · ③ normalise and check the shape
lab_c.pycontinues from lab_b.py
f, tt, Z = signal.spectrogram(x, fs, nperseg=256, noverlap=192,
                              mode="magnitude")
D = 20*np.log10(Z + 1e-8)              # decibels
D = np.clip(D, D.max() - 70, D.max())     # drop the silence floor
D = (D - D.min()) / (D.max() - D.min())    # scale to 0…1, like an image
print("feature shape", D.shape, "range", round(D.min(),2), round(D.max(),2))
plt.imshow(D, origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="magma"); plt.show()
✅

Prints feature shape (129, 247) range 0.0 1.0. That array is now indistinguishable, to a model, from a small greyscale photograph — which is the whole reason this session exists.

1 / 60
C · Reading One — and Feeding a Model 🔍 Explore — why nobody plots the raw magnitudes
explore_c.py
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3))
ax[0].pcolormesh(tt, f, Z)                 # linear
ax[1].pcolormesh(tt, f, 20*np.log10(Z+1e-8))  # dB
plt.show()
print("loudest / typical cell =",
      round(Z.max()/np.median(Z)))
🔎

The peak lines survive a linear scale; everything around them does not. Anything past 10% of the peak lands in the bottom tenth of the colour bar — 86% of what the dB picture shows — so leakage, note transitions and the noise floor go flat black. In dB a component 40 dB down sits at 43% of the bar instead of 1%. Hearing is roughly logarithmic too, so the dB picture is closer to what the sound is actually like.

D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off Key Terms — The Two Resolutions

Window length (L)

/ˈwɪn.doʊ/

Samples per frame — the single knob this whole sub-topic is about.

จำนวน sample ต่อเฟรม — ปุ่มเดียวที่หัวข้อนี้พูดถึง

Frequency resolution (Δf)

/ˈdel.tə ef/

How close two tones can be and still show as two lines: Δf=fs​/L. Session 6's bin spacing, unchanged.

แยกสองความถี่ที่ใกล้กันได้แค่ไหน = fs/L (ระยะห่าง bin จากคาบ 6)

Time resolution (Δt)

/ˈdel.tə tiː/

How precisely you can say when something happened: Δt=L/fs​, the duration of one frame.

บอกเวลาที่เกิดเหตุได้ละเอียดแค่ไหน = L/fs (ความยาวของหนึ่งเฟรม)

The uncertainty product

/ʌnˈsɜː.tən.ti/

Δt⋅Δf=1 — improve one and the other gets worse by the same factor. No setting escapes it.

Δt · Δf = 1 เสมอ · ดีขึ้นด้านหนึ่ง อีกด้านแย่ลงเท่ากัน

⚖️

This is not a limitation of the FFT or of your computer. It is a property of what "a frequency" means: to measure how fast something oscillates, you have to watch it for a while — and while you are watching, you cannot say precisely when.

1 / 60
D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off Two formulas, and they pull in opposite directions

how finely you see frequency — smaller is better

Δf=fs​/L

longer window → Δf shrinks
frequency gets sharper ✓

how finely you see time — smaller is better

Δt=L/fs​

longer window → Δt grows
time gets blurrier ✗

Small is the good direction for both — but a longer window only shrinks one of them · the three pictures from the hook slide, in numbers

L Δf = fs/L Δt = L/fs Δf × Δt
64 125 Hz 8 ms 1
256 31 Hz 32 ms 1
2048 3.9 Hz 256 ms 1
64 → 2048 32× finer 32× coarser unchanged
🔍

The two right-hand sides are reciprocals: L is under the line in one and over it in the other, so every factor you win on one, you lose on the other — 32 and 32 in the last row, not a coincidence. Their product is 1 whatever you choose, which is the next slide.

1 / 60
D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off Their product does not depend on anything you can set
Δt⋅Δf=fs​L​⋅Lfs​​=1

Both L and fs​ cancel. Whatever window you pick, whatever rate you sampled at, the product is one.

The algebra is the easy half: to separate two tones Δf apart you must watch until they drift a whole cycle out of step — frequency resolution is observation time, upside down.

① A requirement becomes a window

Two gearbox fault lines sit 8 Hz apart, so I need Δf≤8 Hz.
Δt=1/Δf=1/8= 0.125 s — the window, straight from the requirement, without thinking about L or fs​ at all.
Only then: at fs​=20 kHz, L=fs​Δt= 2 500 samples.

② Now double the sample rate

Same 0.125 s window at 40 kHz: L doubles to 5 000.
Δf=fs​/L=40000/5000= 8 Hz · Δt= 0.125 s
Both unchanged. The extra rate bought Nyquist — 10 kHz up to 20 kHz — and not one hertz of resolution.

❌

Common mistake: hoping a higher sampling rate will fix a blurry spectrogram. Example ② is why it cannot — fs​ cancels. The only cure is a longer look: Lab D's 900 and 960 Hz tones drift out of step in 17 ms and need a 32 ms window.

1 / 60
D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off There is no best window — only a window that suits the question
🎻

"What note is this?" → long window. You want thin lines you can measure, and the note is not going anywhere.

🥁

"When did that happen?" → short window. You want sharp edges in time and you do not care that the lines are fat.

1 / 60
D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off 🌍 What real systems actually pick — and why
application what it has to resolve fs window L = fs·Δt Δf
speech recognition one vowel, before the next sound starts 16 kHz 25 ms 400 40 Hz
music / tuning a semitone apart at A4 is 26 Hz 44.1 kHz 100 ms 4 410 10 Hz
machine vibration fault lines a few Hz from the shaft rate 25.6 kHz 1 s 25 600 1 Hz

Same trade every time — Δf is just 1/window, so the window column and the Δf column are one decision, not two

🗣️

Speech uses 25 ms because that is roughly how long a vowel holds still — long enough to measure, short enough that the next sound has not started. The window length is a claim about how fast your signal changes, and picking it well means knowing your domain, not knowing more DSP.

🔢

In code you set samples, not milliseconds. L=fs​⋅Δt — the same 25 ms is 400 samples at 16 kHz and ≈1 100 at 44.1 kHz. Libraries usually want a power of two, so speech in practice rounds to 512 (32 ms).

1 / 60
D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off ↩ Which of the three pictures was correct?

All of them. None is wrong — three honest views of one signal, each sharp in a different direction. Look at the badges: every picture wins one and loses one, and the middle one wins nothing outright.

The question "which is correct?" has no answer until someone says what they are looking for. "Which is correct for finding the click?" has one.

🎯

Which is why, in a project report, the window length belongs next to the picture — a spectrogram without its L is an unlabelled measurement. And you cannot opt out: signal.spectrogram(x, fs) with no nperseg still hands you a picture — it just picks 256 on your behalf, without saying so.

1 / 60
D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off
💻 LAB — See both failure modes on one signal
①Build a tone + a click · ② three windows · ③ look at what each one loses
lab_d.pyColab · no downloads needed
t3 = np.arange(0, 1, 1/fs)
z = np.sin(2*np.pi*900*t3) + np.sin(2*np.pi*960*t3)   # two close tones
z[int(0.5*fs):int(0.5*fs)+40] += 6.0                     # one sharp click
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.2))
for a, L in zip(ax, [64, 256, 2048]):
    f, tt, Z = signal.spectrogram(z, fs, nperseg=L, noverlap=L*3//4,
                                  mode="magnitude")
    a.pcolormesh(tt, f, 20*np.log10(Z+1e-8), shading="gouraud")
    a.set_ylim(0, 2000); a.set_title(f"L={L} · Δf={fs/L:.0f}Hz · Δt={1000*L/fs:.0f}ms")
plt.show()
✅

At L = 64 the click is a crisp vertical line but 900 and 960 Hz merge into one fat band (Δf = 125 Hz, and they are only 60 Hz apart). At L = 2048 the two tones separate cleanly (Δf = 3.9 Hz) and the click — 5 ms of signal — is spread across three or four columns, some 150 ms, because a window that long cannot place anything more precisely than itself. Neither picture is lying to you.

1 / 60
D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off 🔍 Explore — check that the product really is 1
explore_d.py
for L in [64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]:
    df, dt = fs/L, L/fs
    sep = "yes" if df < 60 else "no "          # can it split 900 from 960?
    print(f"L={L:5d} | Δf={df:7.1f} Hz | Δt={dt*1000:7.1f} ms"
          f" | product={df*dt:.3f} | splits the tones? {sep}")
🔎

The product column reads 1.000 on every single line — that is the point of the exercise. And the last column flips from no to yes at L = 256 (Δf = 31 Hz), which is the first window fine enough to resolve a 60 Hz gap. You can now answer "what window do I need?" with arithmetic instead of trial and error: pick L>fs​/Δfneeded​, then check the resulting Δt is still short enough for the job.

D · The Time–Frequency Trade-off 🎯 Your Turn — size a window from a specification
🎯

The brief: a gearbox recorded at fs = 20 kHz. Two fault frequencies sit 8 Hz apart and you must tell them apart. The load changes every 2 seconds and you need to know which side of a change each reading falls on.

your_turn_d.pyruns as-is · predict before you run it
fs, block = 20000, 2.0
for gap in (8, 1):                          # the spec, then the tighter spec
    L = -(-fs // gap)                    # smallest L with Δf ≤ gap
    print("%2d Hz apart -> L >= %5d · Δf = %5.2f Hz · Δt = %5.3f s = %2.0f%% of the block"
          % (gap, L, fs/L, L/fs, 100*(L/fs)/block))
# TODO: one sentence — at 1 Hz, what would you change about the RECORDING?
✅

What you should see: 8 Hz apart -> L >= 2500 · Δf = 8.00 Hz · Δt = 0.125 s = 6% of the block — fine. 1 Hz apart -> L >= 20000 · Δf = 1.00 Hz · Δt = 1.000 s = 50% of the block — still under 2 s, but each reading now averages half the block of a machine whose load is changing. The answer to the TODO is about the recording, not the analysis: hold the load steady for longer. No window setting buys resolution the measurement never contained.

Every one of them asks: which frequency, and when?

bearings · gearboxes · pumps · wind turbines

Summary Session Summary
The FFT
not a different transform — the DFT computed by halving repeatedly · N2→Nlog2​N, measured here at ~1800× for N = 1024
The spectrogram
cut into frames, FFT each, stack the columns · time across, frequency up, strength as colour
Reading one
horizontal = steady · vertical = sudden · diagonal = sliding · evenly stacked = a pitch, and the spacing is the note
As a feature
take dB, normalise, and it is an image — which is how audio classification becomes image classification
The trade-off
Δf=fs​/L · Δt=L/fs​ · Δt⋅Δf=1 always — a higher sampling rate does not help
Choosing L
L ≥ fs/Δf, then check Δt · state it beside every spectrogram you publish

🧮Worked Example — How Much Does the FFT Actually Save?

Given

  • a 10-second recording at fs​ = 8000 Hz
  • you want one transform of the whole thing
  • N = 80,000 → round up to 2¹⁷ = 131,072

Find

  • the two operation counts, and the ratio
DefinitionN² = 131,072² ≈ 1.7 × 10¹⁰
FFTN·log₂N = 131,072 × 17 ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶
Ratio1.7 × 10¹⁰ / 2.2 × 10⁶ ≈ 7,700×
Sanityratio ≈ N / log₂N = 131,072 / 17
∴ about 7,700 times less work — for the same answer
🔑

The shortcut worth remembering: the speed-up is roughly N/log2​N, so it keeps growing with the data.

1 / 60
✎Quick Check — Name That Spectrogram⏱ 2 min

A spectrogram shows one bright horizontal line at 400 Hz for the whole recording, plus a faint vertical stripe at t = 3 s that spans every frequency. What was recorded?

✅

A steady 400 Hz tone, with a single click or bump at 3 seconds. Horizontal means unchanging in time; vertical means brief and broadband — a knock, a door, a dropped object, a switch. The two are independent events that happen to share a recording: a tone that ran the whole time, and one instant of something else.

1 / 60
🧮Worked Example — Sizing a Window from a Requirement

Given

  • fs​ = 44,100 Hz (a phone recording)
  • two guitar strings 5 Hz apart must show as two lines

Find

  • (a) the window length L
  • (b) the time resolution it costs
NeedΔf ≤ 5 Hz
(a)L ≥ fs/Δf = 44100/5 = 8,820 → use 16,384
(b)Δt = L/fs = 16384/44100 ≈ 0.37 s
CheckΔt·Δf = 0.37 × 2.7 ≈ 1 ✓
∴ a third of a second per column — fine for a held note
❌

Asking for 5 Hz resolution and millisecond timing. Write both numbers down before you start — that is when an impossible spec is cheap to spot.

1 / 60
✎Quick Check — Would a Better Microphone Help?⏱ 3 min

Your spectrogram cannot separate two tones that are 10 Hz apart. A colleague suggests re-recording at 96 kHz instead of 48 kHz. (a) Does that help? (b) What actually would?

✅

(a) No — it makes it worse. With L unchanged, doubling fs​ doubles Δf from 20 Hz to 40 Hz. (Doubling both fs​ and L keeps Δf the same and buys nothing but bigger files.)  (b) Record for longer and use a longer window — resolution comes from the duration you analyse, not from the sampling rate. A higher rate only raises the highest frequency you can represent (Session 2).

🧮Worked Example — Reading a Spectrogram Out Loud
Shapesthree horizontal lines — all steady
Spacing300 and 600: a fundamental and its 2nd harmonic
Odd one1450 is not a multiple of 300 → not the same source
Timingstarts ≈ 1.6 s, and Δt = 64 ms, so "1.6 s ± 0.06"
∴ new, unrelated 1450 Hz source from 1.6 s
🧭

Note the last step: the window length sets how precisely you may quote the time. Claiming "1.62 s" from 64 ms columns is over-reporting.

Part B 💻 In code — Q5 (the analysis you would actually hand over)

Topics pulled in: FFT cost · frames and hop · reading shapes · Δt·Δf = 1

📋The Case — A Wind-Turbine Gearbox

The situation

  • A vibration sensor records at fs = 25,600 Hz for 60 s.
  • The maintenance manual lists two fault frequencies 12 Hz apart.
  • The turbine changes speed roughly every 5 seconds.
  • The whole file must be analysed on a small on-site computer.

Answer these

  • Q1 — what window length do you need, and what Δt does it cost?
  • Q2 — is that Δt acceptable given the speed changes? Say why.
  • Q3 — one engineer suggests a single FFT of all 60 s instead. What would that give you, and what would it destroy?
  • Q4 — roughly how many FFTs does your spectrogram need, and is that a problem?
💭

Work in order: resolution requirement → window → time cost → check it against how fast the machine changes.

✔Part A — Answers
Q1Δf ≤ 12 Hz → L ≥ 25600/12 ≈ 2,133 → use 4096 · Δt = 4096/25600 = 0.16 s
Q2Yes, comfortably. The machine holds a speed for ~5 s and each column
covers 0.16 s — about 30 columns per operating condition.
Q3One 60 s FFT gives Δf = 1/60 ≈ 0.017 Hz — spectacular resolution —
but it averages every speed together, so each fault line smears across
all the speeds the turbine ran at. Resolution you cannot use.
Q41.5 M samples ÷ 1024-sample hop ≈ 1,500 FFTs of 4096 ≈ 74 M operations
— milliseconds. By the definition it would be ~25 billion. Sub-topic A is why this case is routine.
🧠

Q3 is the one to remember: more resolution is not automatically more information. Averaging across conditions the machine was never in at the same time produces a number that describes no moment at all.

💻Q5 — The Analysis You Would Hand Over
case.pyruns as-is · predict before you run it
fs = 25600
t  = np.arange(0, 60, 1/fs)              # a stand-in for the recording
x  = np.sin(2*np.pi*1200*t) + 0.5*np.sin(2*np.pi*1212*t)*(t >= 30)
x += 0.02*np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=t.size)
def look(L):
    f, tt, Z = signal.spectrogram(x, fs, nperseg=L, noverlap=3*L//4, mode="magnitude")
    b = (f > 1100) & (f < 1300); late = Z[b][:, tt > 40].mean(axis=1)
    r = Z[np.argmin(abs(f - 1212))]; base = np.median(r[tt < 10])
    print("L=%5d Δf=%5.2f Δt=%5.3f s · lines after 40 s: %d · 1212 Hz rises at %.2f s"
          % (L, fs/L, L/fs, len(signal.find_peaks(late, height=late.max()/4)[0]),
             tt[np.argmax(r > 5*base)]))
look(4096); look(512)
✅

What you should see: at L = 4096, Δf=6.25 · lines after 40 s: 2 · 1212 Hz rises at 30.12 s — both faults resolved, onset found. At L = 512, Δf=50.00 · lines: 1 · rises at 0.01 s — merged into one line and a nonsense onset, while the picture still looks perfectly reasonable. Not an error message: just a plausible spectrogram that quietly cannot answer your question.
